title: Repiratory viral testing in the management of febrile infants presenting to Emergency care: A pilot study
official: Repiratory viral testing in the managEment of Febrile INfants presenting to Emergency care
summary:
Background and study aims
Fever is a common reason for young infants to attend an Emergency Department (ED). In babies under 90 days old, a fever can sometimes be a sign of a serious infection, such as meningitis or sepsis. For this reason, young babies with a fever may undergo tests such as blood tests or a lumbar puncture, where a needle is inserted into the lower back to collect a sample of fluid from around the spinal cord. Many babies are also given antibiotics and admitted to hospital.
However, fever in young babies is often caused by a viral infection that does not require antibiotics or invasive tests. Recent evidence suggests that testing for viruses using a simple nose or throat swab may help doctors identify babies who are less likely to have a serious bacterial infection.
Rapid viral tests can provide results within approximately one hour. The REFINE study will investigate whether rapid testing for three common viruses, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) and influenza (flu), could help reduce the number of invasive tests performed, antibiotic use, time spent in the Emergency Department and hospital admissions.
The longer-term aim is to carry out a larger UK-wide trial. Before doing this, a smaller pilot study is needed to find out whether a larger trial can be successfully delivered. The pilot will look at how many families are willing to take part, how healthcare professionals use the rapid viral test, and whether the test appears to affect babies' care.
The study will also explore the views and experiences of parents or caregivers and healthcare professionals regarding rapid viral testing and participation in the research.

Who can participate?
Infants aged between 29 and 90 days who attend hospital with a fever greater than 38°C.

What does the study involve?
Babies taking part will be randomly allocated to one of two groups:
•	Usual care group: Babies will receive the usual care provided by the clinical team, without the rapid viral test being used as part of the study.
•	Rapid viral testing group: Babies will receive usual care and will also have a rapid viral test for RSV, COVID-19 and flu using a nose or throat swabs.
The rapid viral test provides a result within approximately one hour.

Apart from the rapid viral test, the study will not change the care babies receive. Decisions about investigations, treatment, antibiotics and hospital admission will continue to be made by the doctors and nurses looking after the baby.
The research team will collect information to help determine whether a larger UK-wide trial would be possible. This will include information about recruitment, how the rapid test is used by healthcare professionals, and whether it may affect tests, treatment, time spent in the Emergency Department or hospital admission.
Parents or caregivers and healthcare professionals will also be asked about their views and experiences of the rapid viral test and the study.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?  
There may be no direct benefit to babies taking part in this pilot study. However, the information collected will help researchers understand whether rapid viral testing could be used in a larger UK study investigating whether it can safely reduce invasive procedures, antibiotic use, time spent in the Emergency Department and hospital admissions for young babies with fever.

For babies allocated to the rapid viral testing group, the test involves taking a swab from the nose or throat. This may cause brief discomfort or distress.

Where is the study run from?
The REFINE pilot study will be run at Cardiff and Vale University Health Board and the study is being coordinated by  Cardiff University  Clinical Trial Unit. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November  2026 and run until  June  2027.

Who is funding the study?
Health and Care Research Wales 

Who is the main contact?
Angela Strang, REFINE@cardiff.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Infants aged 29 - 90 days with fever ≥ 38.0°C (Fever ≥ 38˚C recorded in ED or in preceding 24 hours by any
thermometer)
Exclusion criteria:
1. Infants born at <32 weeks’ gestation
2. Discharged from hospital more than 7 days after birth
3. Required re-admission to hospital after birth for more than 24 hours and received parenteral antibiotics
4.Nasopharyngeal surgery
5.Infants with a focal bacterial infection (eg, cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis) or clinical bronchiolitis
